nodeData.note: What law is: natural law, positivism, realism, justice and African jurisprudence.

children.note: The study of what law is, where its authority comes from, and how it should relate to morality and justice. It is the "big questions" course of the LLB, and gives you the vocabulary to argue about any rule you meet.

nodeData.note: The study of what law is, where its authority comes from, and how it should relate to morality and justice. It is the "big questions" course of the LLB, and gives you the vocabulary to argue about any rule you meet.

children.note: Legal theory: thinking about law itself rather than one area of rules.

children.topic: The central question: what is law?
children.note: Is a rule law because a ruler commands it, because society accepts it, or because it is just? Each school gives a different answer.

manas.q: What is the central question of jurisprudence?

children.note: Describes what law is and how legal systems work, like a map of the system.
Asks what law ought to be: when is a law just, and when should we obey it?

children.topic: Why a Kenyan student needs it
children.note: Courts interpreting the Constitution 2010 constantly face theory questions: values versus text, custom versus statute, rights versus majority will.
A rule says "no matatu in the CBD". Is it law because the county made it, because people obey it, or only if it is fair? That is jurisprudence in one line.
The oldest school: true law is connected to reason and morality, so an unjust rule is defective as law.
There are moral standards we can discover by reason, and human law should conform to them.

manas.q: What is the core claim of natural law theory?

children.note: Aristotle tied the good to human nature; Cicero described natural law as right reason agreeing with nature.
Thomas Aquinas linked eternal law (God's plan), natural law (our reasoned share of it), divine law (revealed) and human law (made by rulers).

manas.q: Name the kinds of law in Aquinas's scheme.

children.topic: Aquinas: unjust law is no law
children.note: An unjust law keeps only the outward look of law; it is a corruption of law (lex iniusta non est lex).

manas.q: What does "lex iniusta non est lex" mean?

children.note: John Finnis lists seven self-evident goods: life, knowledge, play, aesthetic experience, sociability, practical reasonableness and religion. Law exists to help people pursue them.

children.topic: Fuller: the inner morality of law
children.note: Lon Fuller argued that a system only counts as law if it meets certain procedural standards. This is a "procedural" natural law.
Rules should be general, published, not retroactive, clear, not contradictory, fairly stable, possible to obey, and applied as written.

manas.q: List Fuller's eight principles of legality.

children.note: Law is a social fact: what counts as law depends on how it was made, not on whether it is good.
Law and morality are separate questions. A rule can be valid law and still be unjust.

manas.q: What is the separation thesis?

children.note: Jeremy Bentham, an early positivist, wanted law studied as it is, then reformed by asking what produces the most happiness.
Law is a command from a sovereign whom people habitually obey, backed by a sanction (threat of punishment).

manas.q: How did John Austin define law?

children.note: His theory fits criminal law, but struggles with constitutions, international law and power-giving rules like contracts and wills.
In The Concept of Law (1961), H.L.A. Hart said law joins primary rules (how to behave) with secondary rules (how rules are recognised, changed and applied).

manas.q: What are primary and secondary rules in Hart's theory?

children.note: The master secondary rule that officials use to identify which rules are valid law.

manas.q: What is Hart's rule of recognition?

children.note: Hans Kelsen said each norm gets its validity from a higher norm, ending in an assumed basic norm (Grundnorm).

manas.q: What is Kelsen's Grundnorm?

children.note: Exclusive positivists (Raz) say law is identified by social sources only; inclusive positivists say a system may adopt moral tests.
Famous exchanges that sharpen the natural law versus positivism argument.
Two essays in the Harvard Law Review: Hart defended keeping law and morals apart; Fuller replied that law has a built-in morality.
In 1944 a wife reported her husband's anti-Hitler remarks to be rid of him. After the war a court convicted her, treating the Nazi law she relied on as offending basic justice.

children.topic: Hart vs Fuller on the informer
children.note: Hart said be honest: either punish her using a retroactive law, or let her go, and admit the moral cost. Fuller said the Nazi rules were not true law at all.
Ronald Dworkin argued law is not just rules: judges also apply principles, and the right answer comes from the best moral reading of the law.
A grandson poisoned his grandfather to inherit. The New York court refused him the estate: no one may profit from their own wrong, though no statute said so.

manas.q: What did Riggs v Palmer decide and why did Dworkin use it?

children.note: Dworkin's imaginary perfect judge finds the reading that best fits and justifies the whole law: "law as integrity" (Law's Empire, 1986).
Schools that look at what law does in real life, where it comes from, and whom it serves.
Law is what courts actually do. Study judges, not just rule books.
Oliver Wendell Holmes Jr. saw law as predictions of what courts will in fact decide.

manas.q: How did Holmes describe law?

children.note: American realists who looked behind decisions to the judges themselves and their psychology.
A separate European tradition (Hägerström, Ross, Olivecrona) explaining law by empirical social facts.
Law grows out of a people's history and customs, not from a ruler's will.

children.topic: Savigny: the spirit of the people
children.note: Friedrich Carl von Savigny said each nation's law reflects its Volksgeist and opposed rushing into a German code.

manas.q: What did Savigny mean by Volksgeist?

children.note: Henry Maine's Ancient Law (1861) traced a move from roles fixed by birth and family to relations people choose by agreement.
Study law in light of the society around it.
Roscoe Pound saw law as a tool to balance competing individual and social interests and solve social problems.

manas.q: What did Roscoe Pound mean by social engineering?

children.note: Eugen Ehrlich and the European "free law" thinkers stressed the rules people actually live by.
Law reflects the economy and serves the class that owns the means of production.
The economic base shapes a legal and political superstructure built on top of it.

manas.q: In Marxist theory, is law part of the base or the superstructure?

children.note: Evgeny Pashukanis tied law to commodity exchange and said that under full communism law and state would wither away.
A 1970s US movement: legal decisions are political choices, rules rarely settle cases, and law tends to protect the powerful.

manas.q: What are the main claims of critical legal studies?

children.note: Asks how law has kept women subordinate and how to change it.
Liberal feminists seek real equality; difference feminists want law to recognise real differences; dominance theory (MacKinnon) sees law as male power.

manas.q: Name three strands of feminist legal theory.

children.note: Kimberlé Crenshaw showed that race, sex and class can combine to create disadvantages that single-issue law misses.
Should law enforce morality, and what makes a society just?
Arising from proposals to decriminalise homosexuality in the UK: Lord Devlin said law may enforce shared morality; Hart disagreed.

manas.q: What was the Hart–Devlin debate about?

children.note: John Rawls asked what rules people would choose for society if they did not know their own place in it.
In the "original position" you do not know your class, wealth or talents, so you cannot rig the rules for yourself.

manas.q: What is Rawls's veil of ignorance?

children.note: First, equal basic liberties for all (this comes first). Second, fair equality of opportunity, and inequalities only if they help the worst-off (difference principle).

manas.q: What is the difference principle?

children.note: Libertarian replies: Robert Nozick defended a minimal state; Friedrich Hayek stressed the rule of law and spontaneous order.

children.topic: Example: a land dispute in Kiambu
children.note: Two families claim the same plot. A positivist asks what the register says; a natural lawyer asks what is just; Rawls asks what rule you would accept not knowing which family you are.
African ideas about law and the place of customary law in Kenya today.
Long-standing community practices that become binding because people treat them as obligatory.

manas.q: What is customary law?

children.note: Studies of African customary systems show rules applied flexibly to the facts of each dispute, aiming to restore relationships.
"A person is a person through other persons." Justice focuses on repairing relationships through apology, restitution and reconciliation.
Any law, including customary law, that conflicts with the Constitution is invalid to that extent.

manas.q: What happens to customary law that conflicts with Kenya's Constitution?

children.note: Courts must promote reconciliation, mediation, arbitration and traditional dispute resolution, but not where it breaks the Bill of Rights, justice and morality, or written law.

manas.q: What limits does Article 159 put on traditional dispute resolution?

children.note: Wambui Otieno and her husband's Umira Kager clan fought over where to bury him. The Court of Appeal applied Luo custom and gave the clan the burial.

manas.q: What did the Court of Appeal decide in the S.M. Otieno burial dispute?

children.note: It shows the clash between custom and the individual, and between the historical school and positivist written law.
Add the leading Kenyan decisions from Kenya Law (kenyalaw.org).
Most exam questions are essays: "Discuss" a claim about law.
State the question's claim, explain two or three schools that answer it, compare them, then give your own reasoned view.
"An unjust law is not law. Discuss." Explain Aquinas and Fuller, then Hart's separation thesis, use the grudge informer, then apply to a Kenyan example.
Tie theory to the Constitution 2010: supremacy of the Constitution, customary law, and the courts' value-based interpretation.
Mistakes examiners often see.
Wrong. Positivists say a bad law is still law, but can be criticised and disobeyed on moral grounds.
Austin: commands and sanctions. Hart: rules, including power-giving rules, and the rule of recognition.
Marks come from comparing theories and judging them, not reciting who said what.
